extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students studying remedies and procedure for patent infringement
extracted.subtask_short: action at law for patent infringement
extracted.subtask_description: Legal rules and practical principles governing suits for patent infringement: who may sue, what acts constitute infringement (timing), how damages/profits are measured and awarded, pleading requirements, and related doctrines on assignments and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of profits for infringement of an improved process
rubrics_metrics.description: The question ... is, what advantage did the defendant derive from using the complainant's invention over what he had in using other processes then open to the public, and adequate to enable him to obtain an equally beneficial result? The fruits of that advantage are his profits. They are all the benefits he derived from the existence of the ... invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the recoverable profits by the advantage in cost, skill required, convenience of operation, or marketability the patented process provided over other available processes. It is unimportant what name was given to products except as it affects marketability. If other processes produced equally fit products, only the profits attributable to the patented advantage are recoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: No liability for entire manufacturing profits when process improvement is not sole cause
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of an improved process in a manufacture ... an infringer is not liable to the extent of his entire profits in the manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the infringer's manufacture could achieve similar results by other processes then open to the public, the patentee cannot recover the defendant's entire manufacturing profits; only the portion attributable to the patented improvement is recoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patents do not grant exclusive rights in old constituent elements singly
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent is for an entire process, made up of several constituents. The patentee does not claim to have been the inventor of the constituents. The exclusive use of them singly is not secured to him. What is secured is their use when arranged in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a patent claims a combination or entire process composed of known elements, others remain free to use individual known elements unless the patentee separately claims them. The patentee cannot appropriate each old device singly by virtue of the combination claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoverable profits only when patented element used substantially as claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: He was liable to account for such profits only when he used slow cooling in connection with reheating in the manner described in Whitney's claim substantially, or when extraneous heat was employed to retard the progress of cooling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability to account for profits requires that the defendant employ the patented process or element substantially as claimed, not merely use a similar or incidental technique that exists in other processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits are damages; interest before decree generally not allowable
rubrics_metrics.description: The profits which are recoverable against an infringer of a patent are in fact a compensation for the injury the patentee has sustained ... Though called profits, they are really damages, and unliquidated until the decree is made. Interest is not generally allowable upon unliquidated damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because recoverable profits are treated as unliquidated damages, courts generally do not allow interest prior to the final decree, except in exceptional cases. Lack of wantonness or a favorable PTO determination may justify denying interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts done before patent issuance are not infringements
rubrics_metrics.description: It is obvious that the patent cannot be infringed by anything done when the patent did not exist; and therefore it is no infringement to make or use a machine subsequently patented ... before the patent is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use or manufacture conducted before a patent issues is not an infringement; however, once a patent is granted the right relates back to the invention date and prior users must cease further use after issuance. Acts after issuance are actionable even if previous acts occurred before issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continued use after reissue may be infringement without notice
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party erect and put in use a patented machine, during the existence of a defective patent which is afterwards surrendered, it will be an infringement of the new and reissued patent, if he continues the use of such machine after the renewal; and it seems that no notice is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a patent is surrendered and reissued to cure defects, continued use of the machine after reissue may constitute infringement; actual notice of reissue is not necessarily required to sustain liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending suits fall with surrender and reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: Suits for infringement pending at the time of the surrender and reissue of letters-patent fall with such surrender, because the foundation on which they rested no longer exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original patent is surrendered before issuance of a reissued patent, pending infringement suits based on the surrendered patent are typically abated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages may be recovered for infringement during Patent Office record destruction period
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may recover damages for an infringement during the time which intervened between the destruction of the Patent Office by fire ... and the restoration of the records under the act of March 3, 1837.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory restoration of records can preserve patentee rights to damages during periods in which public records were unavailable due to extraordinary events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory remedy: action on the case for damages (Act of July 4, 1836 §14)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of Congress of July 4, 1836, c. 357, § 14, provides that damages may be recovered for an infringement by 'an action on the case,' — a remedy which exists equally at common law, for the violation of the right secured by letters-patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages for patent infringement are recoverable in an action on the case (tort-based action), per statute and common law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may bring suit: persons 'interested' in the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The action shall be brought in the name or names of the person or persons interested, whether as patentee, assignees, or as grantees of the exclusive right within and throughout a specified part of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs must be persons holding the legal or exclusive interest (patentee, assignee, or territorial grantee) at the relevant time; the statute contemplates various modes of holding interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee of a sectional (territorial) exclusive right may sue in own name
rubrics_metrics.description: Formerly, the grantee for a particular district could not bring an action on the patent in his own name. But the statute has made him a party interested in the patent, and consequently, in his own district, he may sue in his own name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignee granted an exclusive right within a specified territory may maintain an infringement action in that territory in his own name, provided the assignment conveys an exclusive territorial monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment must convey entire and unqualified monopoly for territorial suit
rubrics_metrics.description: But in order that the assignee of a sectional interest may sue in his own name, the assignment must clearly convey to him the entire and unqualified monopoly which the patentee held in the specified territory, excluding the patentee himself as well as others; for any assignment short of this is a mere license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the assignment does not transfer the full exclusive territorial interest (e.g., reserves rights to the grantor), it will be treated as a license and may not support a suit in the assignee's name alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions by assignee for a limited number of machines can be proper
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been recently held that the grant of a right to construct and use fifty machines within certain localities, reserving to the grantor the right to construct and to license others to construct, but not to use them therein, was the grant of an exclusive right under the patent ... and that consequently the suit was rightly brought in the name of the assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may treat certain narrowly limited grants (e.g., a number of machines in localities with specific usage limits) as exclusive rights permitting suit by assignee, depending on the reservation language and effect on exclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may sue on behalf of exclusive licensee damaged by infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: An action may properly be brought by the patentee in behalf of one to whom he has granted an exclusive license and who has been damaged by the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the licensee has suffered damage, the patentee can pursue relief on the licensee's behalf in appropriate circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint owners and suits among co-owners
rubrics_metrics.description: One joint owner of a patent can bring an action of infringement against his co-owner for making and selling machines in a manner which does not respect his rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint ownership does not bar an infringement suit between co-owners when one acts in violation of the other's rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must be brought by assignee if whole interest had been assigned
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patentee has assigned his whole interest, either before or after the patent was taken out, the action can only be brought in the name of the assignee;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee has completely assigned the patent (the whole interest), the assignee holds the right to sue exclusively; partial assignments (undivided part) require appropriate joint naming to represent whole interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where assignment is of undivided part, joinder of patentee and assignee required
rubrics_metrics.description: But where the assignment is of an undivided part of the interest, the action should be brought in the joint names of the patentee and the assignee, as representing the whole interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To represent the entire interest and recover full damages, plaintiffs whose ownership is divided should join appropriate parties to the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee of a severable portion may sue alone in some jurisdictions/cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In a recent English case, it was held that the assignee of a separate and distinct portion of a patent may sue for an infringement of that patent, without joining one who has an interest in another part, the damages to be recovered accruing to the former alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English authority supports allowing an assignee of a self-contained, severable portion of a patent to sue alone for infringements of that portion; courts recognize differing approaches and practical considerations (joinder, prejudice to defendants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee must be interested at time infringement committed to recover past damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The true meaning of the word 'interested' ... is that the right of action is given to the person or persons owning the exclusive right at the time the infringement is committed. Subsequent sale and transfer of the exclusive right are no bar to an action to recover damages for an infringement committed before such sale and transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claimant can only recover damages for infringements that occurred while they owned the exclusive right; subsequent assignees cannot recover damages for prior infringements unless they owned the interest at the time the cause of action accrued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of agreed but unmade assignment; recording
rubrics_metrics.description: If the assignment has not been made, but has been merely agreed to be made, the action should be in the name of the patentee, the assignee not having the interest until the assignment has been made and recorded. But it may be recorded at any time after the suit is brought and before trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignment only vests the legal interest once executed; plaintiffs should bring suit in the name of the party holding legal title at the time of suit initiation, though courts permit recording of assignments before trial to cure technical defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporations and executors can be sued or can sue
rubrics_metrics.description: An action for an infringement may be maintained against a corporation. Where several persons are appointed as executors ... such executor can maintain an action for infringement ... without joining his co-executors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate defendants are proper; executors who have taken out letters of administration or been vested with the legal title may sue without joining co-executors in practical circumstances; surrender and reissue to executor vests exclusive legal title enabling suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration (pleading) must show title and essential matters with convenient certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration, in an action for the infringement of a patent, should show a title in the plaintiff, with convenient certainty; and should set forth all the matters which are of the essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleadings must allege the plaintiff's title, novelty and utility of the invention, that it was not in public use or on sale with plaintiff's consent before application, and that the plaintiff obtained letters-patent in due form. These are essential to establish prima facie right; specific time of invention need not be alleged beyond being before application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration should aver original and first inventor and patent formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration should commence with a recital that the plaintiff was 'the original and first inventor' ... and should aver that the subject-matter was 'new and useful,' 'not known or used before the plaintiff's invention or discovery,' and 'not at the time of his application for a patent in public use or on sale with his consent or allowance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though letters-patent are evidence, the declaration must independently allege invention, novelty, non-publication, and proper procurement of the patent, including that it was obtained under seal and countersigned by appropriate officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizenship averment: practice and prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether it is necessary to aver the citizenship of the patentee has never been determined. In practice it is generally done, and it is safer to do so than to omit an averment which might on demurrer be held to be essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not strictly resolved, plead citizenship in the declaration to avoid potential demurrer or jurisdictional objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of covenants and extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: A covenant by a patentee, made prior to the law authorizing extensions, that the covenantee should have the benefit of any improvement in the machinery, or alteration or renewal of the patent, did not include the extension by an administrator under the act of 1836; that it must be construed to include only renewals obtained upon the surrender of a patent on account of a defective specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construing pre-statute covenants, courts limit the covenant's scope to types of renewals and improvements reasonably within the parties' contemplation at the time; later statutory extensions may be excluded.
